title: Taking the best step now
objectives: Recognise when a greedy choice is safe, and find a case where it fails.
Implement greedy change and earliest-finish scheduling, and prove the schedule optimal by exchange.

screens.title: Change for 87p
screens.prose: You owe 87p and hold plenty of every UK coin: 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p and 50p.
screens.question: What is the fewest coins that make 87p?

hints.text: Start with the largest coin that fits.
50p fits once into 87p.
50p leaves 37p; 20p leaves 17p; 10p leaves 7p; 5p leaves 2p; 2p leaves 0. Five coins.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the largest coin that fits, again and again.

byKey.ones: You used 1p coins only. Bigger coins cover the amount in far fewer.
byKey.six: You used six coins. Check each step takes the largest coin that still fits.

explain.text: At each step you took the largest coin that fits and never went back. For UK coins this always gives the fewest coins.

screens.title: Odd coins
screens.prose: Another country has only 1, 3 and 4 coins. You owe 6.
screens.question: What is the fewest coins that make 6?

hints.text: Try the largest coin first, then try without it.
The 4 leaves 2, which needs two 1s.
4 + 1 + 1 is three coins. 3 + 3 is two.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Do not stop at the first answer you find.

byKey.greedy: You took the largest coin first: 4 + 1 + 1. Two 3s make 6 with one coin fewer.
byKey.six: You used 1s only. A 3 or a 4 covers more at once.

explain.text: Taking the 4 first felt best, but it left 2, which only 1s can cover. Two 3s do better. The best step now is not always best overall.

screens.title: Where it fails
screens.prose: Always taking the largest coin that fits is a **greedy** method: the best step now, never undone. The table shows how many coins greedy uses with 1, 3 and 4.
screens.question: Tap every amount where you can beat greedy. Select all that apply.

hints.text: For each amount, look for a way with fewer coins, using 3s.
Amount 6 is the one you just met.
6 = 3 + 3 (2 coins, not 3). 10 = 4 + 3 + 3 (3 coins, not 4). Every other row is already the fewest.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each row for a way with fewer coins.

byKey.only6: You found 6. Try 10 too: greedy gives 4 + 4 + 1 + 1, but 4 + 3 + 3 uses three coins.
byKey.r8: 9 needs three coins either way: 4 + 4 + 1 or 3 + 3 + 3.
byKey.r4: 5 is 4 + 1, two coins, and no single coin makes 5.

explain.text: Greedy is right for 8 of these 10 amounts. A method that works on most cases can still be wrong. With UK coins it is right for every amount, but that needs a reason, not examples.

screens.title: Write greedy change
screens.prose: Return the coins greedy takes, largest first. The coins may come in any order. If greedy cannot finish the amount exactly, return `None`.
screens.question: Write `coins_greedy(amount, coins)`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They try UK coins, the 1, 3, 4 system (greedy's three coins, not the best two) and coins given unsorted. Others try an amount of 0, an amount greedy cannot finish, US-style coins and a large amount.

hints.text: Go through the coins from largest to smallest.
Greedy's answer for 6 is three coins: 4, 1, 1.
For each `c` in `sorted(coins, reverse=True)`, append `c` while `amount >= c` and subtract it. If `amount` is not 0 at the end, return `None`.

feedback.correct: This is greedy, faithfully, including where it is not the best.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 gives the coins unsorted. Sort them largest first.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is an amount of 0, which needs no coins: return `[]`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 is 3 with coins 5 and 2. Greedy takes 2 and is stuck on 1, so return `None`.

explain.text: The code is short and fast. Whether it gives the fewest coins depends on the coin system. It does for UK coins, but not for 1, 3, 4 or for 1, 10, 25.

screens.title: One meeting room
screens.prose: Seven meetings want one room tomorrow. Two can share the room only if one ends before or as the other starts.
screens.question: What is the largest number of meetings the room can hold?

hints.text: Which meeting would you pick first to leave the most room afterwards?
B ends earliest, at 10:30.
Keep B (ends 10:30), then C (ends 11:30), then E (ends 13:00), then F (ends 14:30): four.

feedback.correct: Four, for example B, C, E and F.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for meetings that end early.

byKey.one: You took A, the first to start. It blocks the room from 9:00 to 15:00.
byKey.three: Three fit, but a fourth can too. Pick meetings that end early.
byKey.all: Several meetings overlap, so not all seven fit.

explain.text: Picking the meeting that ends first leaves the most time free. Then pick the next that starts after it ends, and so on. That gives four.

screens.title: Earliest finish first
screens.prose: Write the greedy rule you just used. Intervals are `(start, end)` pairs in any order. Touching intervals, where one ends as the next starts, do not clash.

state.caption: Greedy keeps B, C, E, F

screens.question: Write `max_meetings(intervals)`: the most intervals that can be kept with no two overlapping.

tests.call: max_meetings([(i, i + 2) for i in range(100000)])

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. They include the diary, an empty list, one meeting, touching meetings and all overlapping. Others have a long meeting around short ones, a case where shortest-first fails, the diary reversed, repeats and 100,000 intervals.

hints.text: Sort by end time, then walk through once.
B ends first, so it is kept first.
Sort by `end`. Keep `last_end` (start at minus infinity). For each `(s, e)`: if `s >= last_end`, count it and set `last_end = e`.

feedback.correct: Sorting is $O(n \log n)$ and the walk is $O(n)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects 4. If you got 1, you sorted by start: the long meeting A came first. If you got 3, a meeting that starts as the last one ends was refused: use `>=`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has three touching meetings and expects 3: a meeting may start the moment the last one ends.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 is an empty list, which holds 0 meetings.

explain.text: One sort and one pass. Touching counts as no clash because of `>=`. Next we check why this greedy choice is always optimal, not just here.

screens.title: First come, first served
screens.prose:
A colleague sorts by start time instead: `sorted` on pairs orders by the first item.

```python
for s, e in sorted(intervals):
    if s >= last_end:
        count += 1
        last_end = e
```

On tomorrow's diary it returns 1.

state.caption: Sorted by start, A comes first

screens.question: Why does it return 1 when 4 meetings fit?

options.text: A starts first, so it is kept, and it blocks the room until 15:00
It treats touching meetings as clashing
options.why: `s >= last_end` lets touching meetings share. The trouble is which meeting it keeps first.

options.text: It should sort by length instead
options.why: Shortest first fails too: with (1, 5), (4, 7), (6, 10) it keeps only the middle one, but two fit.

options.text: No greedy method can solve this
options.why: Earliest finish first is greedy and always optimal. The sort key is the problem.

hints.text: Which meeting does the loop keep first?
A runs from 9:00 to 15:00.
Sorted by start, A comes first and is kept. Every other meeting starts before 15:00, so none fits after it, and G clashes too.

feedback.correct: Starting early says nothing about leaving room.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace the first meeting kept.

byKey.touch: You blamed touching meetings. The loop keeps A first, and A blocks everything.
byKey.short: You switched to shortest first. That also fails: (4, 7) blocks both (1, 5) and (6, 10).
byKey.greedy: You gave up on greedy. Sorting by end time makes it always optimal.

explain.text: What matters is how much of the day a choice leaves free, and that is decided by its end time. Sorting by start, or by length, can pick a meeting that blocks several others.

screens.title: Why earliest finish is safe
screens.prose: We show some largest schedule starts with the meeting that finishes first. This is an **exchange argument**: swap our greedy choice into an optimal answer and show nothing is lost.

state.caption: g = B, the first to finish

screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: Let $g$ be the meeting that finishes first, and $O$ a largest schedule
Let $o$ be the first meeting in $O$; $g$ ends no later than $o$, because $g$ ends first of all
Every other meeting of $O$ starts when $o$ ends or later, so no earlier than $g$ ends
Swap $o$ for $g$: no clash, same size, so the result is still a largest schedule
So some largest schedule starts with $g$; drop what clashes with $g$ and repeat on the rest

hints.text: Start by naming the greedy choice and an optimal schedule.
B is $g$ here.
Name $g$ and $O$. Compare $g$ with $O$'s first meeting. Show the rest of $O$ still fits after $g$. Swap. Repeat.

feedback.correct: Swapping in the greedy choice never makes the schedule smaller.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name things, compare, then swap.

explain.text: The swap keeps the size and removes no room for later meetings. So the first greedy choice is safe, and the same argument applies to what is left. That proves earliest finish first is optimal for every diary.

screens.title: Whole trades only
screens.prose: You have £10,000 to put into three trades. With part-sized trades, greedy by profit per pound gives £460: all of A, then £4,000 of B. Now each trade must be taken whole or not at all.
screens.question: What is the largest expected profit with whole trades only, in pounds?

hints.text: Greedy takes A first. What fits after it?
A uses £6,000, leaving £4,000.
After A, neither B nor C fits: £300. Skipping A, B and C fit together: £400.

feedback.correct: B and C: £400, more than greedy's £300.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try leaving out the best trade per pound.

byKey.greedy: You took A first, as greedy does. Then nothing else fits; B and C together earn more.
byKey.frac: £460 needs part of B. With whole trades only, that is not allowed.
byKey.all: All three need £16,000, more than you have.

explain.text: With parts allowed (fractional knapsack), greedy by value per pound is optimal. With whole items (0/1 knapsack), it fails, because a good item can waste the space around it. The 0/1 version needs dynamic programming, in graphs and DP.

screens.title: Filling a market order
screens.prose: You send a market order to buy 1,000 shares. The book fills it from the cheapest ask upwards: the greedy choice, and the best one for a single order.
screens.question: What does the order cost in total, in pounds?

hints.text: Take 300 at the best ask, then move up a level.
The first two levels hold 800 shares.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill level by level from the cheapest ask.

byKey.top: You priced all 1,000 at the best ask. Only 300 are offered there.
byKey.avg: You priced every share at a level you did not reach, or averaged the levels. Weight each price by the shares taken.

explain.text: For one order, cheapest first is optimal: any other fill swaps a cheaper share for a dearer one. That is the exchange argument again. Spreading a large order over time is another problem, where greedy can fail.

screens.title: Picking strategies
screens.prose:
You may run two of three strategies, equal weights, equal volatility. Their Sharpe ratios are A 1.5, B 1.4, C 1.0. A and B have correlation 0.95; C is uncorrelated with both. For two such strategies
$$S_p = \frac{S_1 + S_2}{\sqrt{2 + 2\rho}}.$$
screens.question: Greedy picks the two best Sharpe ratios, A and B. Which pair has the higher $S_p$?

options.text: A and B: they have the two best Sharpe ratios
options.why: You picked greedily by Sharpe ratio. Correlation 0.95 means B adds almost nothing A does not already give.
The denominators differ: $\sqrt{3.9}$ for A and B, $\sqrt 2$ for A and C.
B and C give $2.4/\sqrt 2 \approx 1.70$, less than A and C.

hints.text: Work out the denominator for each pair.
A and B move almost together.

feedback.correct: Diversification beats the second-best Sharpe ratio here.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute both $S_p$ values.

explain.text: Greedy by Sharpe ratio ignores how strategies move together. The pair's risk depends on correlation, so the best pair is not the two best singles. Portfolio choice needs the whole covariance, not one number per strategy.

ideas: A greedy method takes the best-looking step now and never undoes it.
It can be optimal, as earliest finish first is. But a single counterexample, such as 6 with coins 1, 3 and 4, sinks it.
An exchange argument proves a greedy choice safe: swapping it into an optimal answer loses nothing.

formula.name: Interval scheduling
formula.tex: \text{sort by end; keep } (s, e) \text{ if } s \ge \text{last end}

summary.trap: Trusting greedy because it worked on the first examples, or sorting meetings by start instead of finish.

options.why: You treated touching meetings as a clash. With `s >= last_end`, 10:00 to 11:00 can follow 9:00 to 10:00.
An empty list sorts to an empty list, and the loop simply does not run.
With no meetings there is nothing to count.

feedback.correct: No meetings, then two that touch.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Handle each call on its own.

quiz.prose: Capacity 10. Items: weight 4 value 20, weight 6 value 18, weight 5 value 10. You may take parts of items.
quiz.question: What is the largest total value?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank the items by value per unit of weight.

byKey.whole: You took the two lightest items whole: 20 and 10. Rank by value per unit of weight instead: 5, 3 and 2.
byKey.best: You added every value. Only 10 units of weight fit.

quiz.prose: A greedy rule gave the best answer on the first three examples you tried.
quiz.question: What does that show?

options.text: Nothing yet: you need a proof, such as an exchange argument, or a check of every case

options.why: Greedy with coins 1, 3 and 4 is right for amounts 1 to 5, then fails at 6.

options.text: The rule is optimal for small inputs only
options.why: Examples say nothing about the cases you did not try, small or large.
It may well be right. Examples alone cannot settle it either way.

feedback.correct: Examples can refute a greedy rule, never prove it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can a few examples rule out a failure elsewhere?

explain.text: One counterexample is enough to sink a greedy rule. To trust one, show that swapping its choice into any optimal answer loses nothing.
